theme: The heavens and the law, creation and word declare God’s glory
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 19. It is a psalm in two halves, one about God’s glory in the heavens and one about his glory in his word. Notice how the psalmist connects them.
settingTheScene: Psalm 19 is a psalm of David, and C. S. Lewis called it among the greatest poems in the Psalter. It moves from creation to Scripture to the heart. It stands at a fitting place in this unit: wisdom literature teaches that God’s world and God’s word fit together. Proverbs says that God made the world by wisdom, and this psalm shows how the world and the law both tell of him.
observation: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork” (v. 1).
“Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge” (v. 2).
“There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard” (v. 3).
“In them he has set a tent for the sun” (v. 4).
“The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (v. 7).
“More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb” (v. 10).
“Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults” (v. 12).
“Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer” (v. 14).
interpretation:
The first half is a hymn to the silent voice of creation. The sky speaks without words, and its message goes out to all the earth. The sun is described as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, running its course with joy. Creation is a constant witness. It tells us that there is a God, that he is glorious, and that he is powerful. Paul uses this psalm to say that no one is without a witness (Romans 10:18).

But creation’s testimony, however clear, is limited. It tells of God’s glory, but it does not tell us how to know him or be forgiven. So the psalm turns, in verse 7, to the law of the LORD. Six names for God’s word, six descriptions, and six effects fill the second section. The law is perfect, reviving the soul. The testimony is sure, making wise the simple. The precepts are right, rejoicing the heart. The commandment is pure, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the LORD is clean, enduring forever. The rules are true and righteous. God’s word does what the heavens cannot: it restores, it instructs, it gives joy.

The word is also better than wealth and sweeter than honey. The psalmist treasures it. But it also warns: “By them is your servant warned; in keeping them there is great reward.”

The third section is personal. Having seen God’s glory in the heavens and the word, the psalmist sees himself. He realizes that he cannot see his own faults. “Who can discern his errors?” He asks for cleansing from hidden sins and for restraint from presumptuous ones. And the psalm ends with the most beloved prayer: “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.”

The movement is from creation, to Scripture, to the heart. The glory of God, rightly seen, makes us aware of our need for him.
connection: Romans 1:19-20 and 10:18 draw on this psalm’s picture of creation’s witness. Hebrews 1:1-2 says God has spoken by his Son. John 1:14 shows the Word made flesh, who is the fullest revelation of God’s glory. Jesus said, “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:63). The “redeemer” of the last verse is fulfilled in Christ (Titus 2:14).
application:
Step outside today and let the sky speak. Thank God for what you see.

Read verses 7 to 9 slowly. Pick the description of God’s word that you most need right now.

Pray verse 14 as you start your day.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for speaking through both creation and his word.
Ask him to cleanse you from hidden faults and keep you from presumption.
Pray Psalm 19:14 as your own prayer.
